front: What does a curly (double-headed) arrow show?
back: Movement of an electron pair: tail at a lone pair or bond, head at the atom where the new bond forms (or where a leaving pair goes).

front: Why is the C in a halogenoalkane attacked by nucleophiles?
back: The halogen is more electronegative, making C–X polar: C is δ+ and attracts the nucleophile’s lone pair.
CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ (warm, aqueous; ethanol forms).

front: Rate of substitution: chloro-, bromo-, iodoalkanes?
back: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl: C–I is the weakest bond, so iodide is the best leaving group (bond strength outweighs polarity).
CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br (bromoethane), room temperature.

front: Why do alkenes react with electrophiles?
back: The C=C π bond is a region of high electron density that attracts electrophiles; the weaker π bond breaks.

front: (HL) Formation of [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ as a Lewis acid–base reaction?
back: Each H₂O (Lewis base) donates a lone pair to Cu²⁺ (Lewis acid), forming six coordination bonds.

front: (HL) BF₃ + NH₃ — which is the Lewis acid?
back: BF₃ (B has an incomplete octet, accepts the pair); NH₃ donates its lone pair forming H₃N→BF₃.
Every Brønsted–Lowry base is a Lewis base (accepts H⁺ using a lone pair), but Lewis acids need not contain H (e.g. BF₃, AlCl₃, metal ions).

front: (HL) Steps of the SN2 mechanism (OH⁻ + bromoethane)?
back: Arrow from OH⁻ lone pair to δ+ C (attack from the side opposite Br); arrow from C–Br bond to Br; one pentacoordinate transition state; Br⁻ leaves; inversion.
Step 1 (slow): C–Br breaks heterolytically → tertiary carbocation + Br⁻. Step 2 (fast): OH⁻ lone pair attacks the planar C⁺ from either side.

front: (HL) Why are tertiary carbocations most stable?
back: Three alkyl groups push electron density towards C⁺ (positive inductive effect), spreading the charge.

front: (HL) Effect of solvent on SN1 vs SN2?
back: Protic solvents (water, alcohols) stabilise the carbocation and halide ion → favour SN1. Aprotic solvents don’t solvate the nucleophile strongly → favour SN2.

front: (HL) Why is SN1 rate independent of [OH⁻]?
back: The nucleophile is not involved in the slow rate-determining step (ionisation of RX).

front: (HL) Why does benzene undergo substitution, not addition?
back: Substitution keeps the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it (lose delocalisation energy).
